news.title: Iran should reduce uranium enrichment capacity to end war with US — vice president
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 7. /TASS/. Iranian authorities should significantly reduce their uranium enrichment capacity in order to end the war with the United States, US Vice President JD Vance said in an interview with Reuters.

"If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue [when ending the conflict]," Vance said. "I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity."

He said the United States remained open to reaching an agreement but would demand concrete concessions from Iran in the nuclear sphere. "We’re not going to trade words for actions," the vice president said. In his view, the situation is complicated by the fact that Washington is unsure who makes decisions in Tehran. Vance said the United States was holding talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. However, he claimed, it was unclear how much influence they wield within Iran’s power structure. "One of the things we picked up on is it’s not totally clear how their country makes decisions," Vance said.

The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding envisaging an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements in what concerned the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.

The Donald Trump administration recently signaled an end to any large-scale use of force against Iran and a transition to putting economic pressure on the Islamic Republic through sanctions instead.
news.summary: JD Vance expressed concern over Iran's possession of highly enriched fuel and added that the US would demand concrete concessions from Iran in the nuclear sphere
news.author: Tass

news.title: Yemen is spiralling into another civil war that could swiftly engulf in the entire region
news.text:
The Middle East has seen many explosions of violence in recent years. But while the US-Iran war has grabbed the headlines this year, the rapidly escalating conflict between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia risks becoming just as consequential for the region. 

The complexity of Yemen’s internal conflict cannot be underestimated. The violence is linked to two major regional powers – Iran and Saudi Arabia – as well as the ongoing US-Israel confrontation with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz. 

Iran backs the Houthis (also known as Ansar Allah or Partisans of God), while Saudi Arabia supports the Yemeni government (known as the Presidential Leadership Council or PLC). The United States is also standing beside its de facto ally, the Saudis, while Russia and China are aligned with Iran. 

And Riyadh’s other regional allies, Turkey and Pakistan, have just agreed to activate their newly signed mutual defence pact and deploy troops to help defend Saudi Arabia if it’s attacked again. 

Given how many actors are involved, the conflict could quickly spiral out of control and engulf the entire region, further destabilising global fuel supplies.

Houthis gaining ground

The US-Iran war has reached a stalemate in recent months. Tehran remains adamant that it controls the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for 20% of the world’s daily supply of oil and liquefied natural gas before the war. And US President Donald Trump has been running hot and cold about how to end the conflict. Neither America’s military might, nor its maximum economic pressure, has worked so far.

Tehran’s Houthi allies, who control one-third of Yemen (including the capital Sanaa), entered the fray to support Iran earlier this year. They have tightened their control of the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. 

And they have made territorial gains in Yemen since July, with the aim of taking over the whole country, while also attacking Saudi oil facilities, tankers and its main airport in Riyadh. An attack in recent days again halted the pumping of oil through the East-West Pipeline, which Riyadh has been using to export oil via Bab al Mandab since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. 

Yemeni and Saudi forces have launched a counteroffensive in recent days in an attempt to retake all the territory held by the Houthis, raising the spectre of a return to a major civil war and a potentially dire humanitarian crisis for Yemenis.

Riyadh has asked Washington to carry out airstrikes on the Houthis, but Trump has declined the request to get actively involved, instead offering support from US intelligence and military analysts in the country. 

Trump has been disinclined to expand the US-Iran war and get the US embroiled in another conflict while the potential for a restart of the war with Iran remains very real. 

In addition, despite his denials that he is concerned, Trump will no doubt be aware of the impact of the Iran war on American consumers, with higher petroleum prices and cost of living pressures. His Republican Party is urgently trying to shore up its voter base with the midterm elections now just a month away.

Without direct US involvement, Riyadh has looked for support from its new security partners, Pakistan and Turkey. Before committing to deploy military forces to Saudi Arabia this week, the two had appeared cautious about getting involved – caught between the need to support Saudi Arabia and not to offend Iran and its strategic partners, Russia and China. 

The renewed conflict has already taken a very heavy toll on the Yemeni people, with more than 800 killed, 3,000 injured and 158,000 displaced. This comes on the top of the hundreds of thousands of people who have died since the civil war and Saudi-led intervention began in 2014–15. These deaths were due to fighting, as well as indirect impacts such as hunger, disease, and lack of health services and infrastructure.

Where is this going?

The worse the fighting becomes in Yemen, the greater the impact on the world economy.

While the Strait of Hormuz remains partially inoperable due to the fear of ships being attacked, some tankers have managed to sail through after making deals with Iran’s new Persian Gulf Strait Authority, or with US escort protection. 

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, recently claimed 13 million barrels of crude oil were getting through the strait daily. This has been disputed by Iran. 

On October 4, Iran’s parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the strait will not reopen fully until the US meets Iranian demands. These include a ceasefire on all fronts, the lifting of the US blockade of Iranian ports and the unfreezing of Iran’s assets. 

And after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports and started attacking Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea in July, disruptions in the global oil supply are expected to worsen.

At the root of this expanding and multi-dimensional crisis is the US war of choice against Iran. If Trump does escalate that conflict with more lethal force, Tehran is prepared to retaliate. It has warned the US’ Arab allies in the Gulf they could be targeted more severely than before.

The overall situation remains very explosive, unless Washington and Tehran pull back from the brink and opt for a negotiated deal. This seems like a distant goal, but it is still possible.
news.summary: Turkey and Pakistan are poised to send troops to Saudi Arabia, but so far the Trump administration has avoided getting involved.

news.title: Paramount and Warner Bros Merge into One Hollywood Giant
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles. The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal. The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation.Why Skydance Corp.? Who's behind the new behemoth?The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros. The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through. "Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump. Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max. Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. news.title: Mixing up countries can cause a lot of confusion
news.text:
Melvin Durai

If you’re a fan of Donald Trump, you’ll be glad to know that India has been on his mind lately. In fact, he posted about India on social media on Oct 4: “125 Million People voted today in the first round of India’s Presidential Election. The results came out shortly after the vote closed, on the SAME DAY!” His Truth Social post puzzled many people, but they quickly realised that Trump had mixed up India and Brazil. He meant to compliment Brazil’s election process, while denigrating what he considers vote rigging in America, but India was apparently on his mind. Trump soon deleted the erroneous post—one of his aides may have pointed out the mistake—but not before the post had been captured in screenshots. For Trump critics, it was proof that the president was losing his mind.

For Trump’s supporters, it was proof that Democrats were occasionally hacking into his Truth Social account. You may think that this was just a simple mistake, but when a country’s leader starts mixing up names, it can cause a lot of confusion. Trump (speaking to reporters): “Before I talk about my new economic initiatives, I want everyone to know that I am very optimistic about a peace agreement between Russia and India. I have spoken to both leaders and they seem very willing to do it.” Reporter: “Do you mean Ukraine?” Trump: “Yes, yes, Ukraine. Of course I mean Ukraine. I am very optimistic about a peace agreement between Ukraine and India. I spoke to both leaders.” Reporter: “You spoke to Prime Minister Modi?” Trump: “Yes, I spoke to him. He is at peace with the idea of peace. I didn’t have to do much convincing. I am good at peace. It comes naturally to me, and one of these days, the Nobel Prize committee will realize it too.” Mixing up names during a social media post or speech may result in little more than ridicule, but there’s always a chance that Trump will wake up one day and decide to bomb the wrong country. He will summon Pete Hegseth, Secretary of War, into the White House to give him the instructions. Trump: “We need to act fast. Just keep bombing Algeria until they agree to do something about all their online scam artists.” Hegseth: “Algeria? Sir, do you mean Nigeria.” Trump: “Algeria, Nigeria, what’s the difference? Aren’t they both in Africa?” Hegseth: “Yes, they’re both in Africa, but they’re different countries. Africa is a large continent.” Trump: “You think I don’t know that? I know all about Africa. Now please go ahead and bomb Niger.” Hegseth: “You mean Nigeria?” Trump: “Stop correcting me! Just pick a country and bomb it. I need to get everyone’s attention away from the economy.” It’s one thing to mistake Niger for Nigeria; it’s quite another to mistake India for Brazil. They’re not even on the same continent, but to Trump’s credit, they’re at least in the same hemisphere. Some Trump critics believe that the 80-year-old president is suffering from cognitive decline and his brain is just not working as well as it used to. This assumes that a much younger Trump, perhaps in his mid-forties, would be able to find Brazil on a map.

Perhaps he would, but he’d surely be stumped by Niger. I know a few people in their eighties and none of them would mistake India for Brazil. Then again, none of them would be posting dozens of messages on social media every day. They’ve got more important things to do, such as reading books and spending time with their grandchildren. If only Trump could find something important to do.

news.title: Hundreds arrested in school protests as Macron summons ministers
news.text:
PARIS: Mass protests over decrepit conditions at France’s high schools descended into sporadic violence Tuesday, leading to nearly 500 arrests and prompting President Emmanuel Macron to call an emergency meeting.

The protests started in late September with students blocking entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds over complaints of dilapidated facilities and teacher shortages.

US President Donald Trump weighed in on Tuesday to blame the unrest in France on “mass migration” and Islam, as he pushed his global right-wing narrative ahead of tough midterm elections at home.

In France, parents, teachers and union workers joined the high school students’ movement in the capital Paris and other cities.

The interior ministry said 256,000 people protested nationwide, while union organisers put the figure at 450,000.

Macron was expected to meet top officials late Tuesday, including Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and Education Minister Edouard Geffray, in response to the unrest, a government source said.

At least 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were wounded on Tuesday, the interior ministry announced.

‘Wants to be heard’

Rights groups, unions and the students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force.

A teenager lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade.

A 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the face with a tear gas grenade at such close range that he lost several teeth. A policeman was charged Tuesday over that incident.

“Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard,” 19-year-old Lilia told AFP at a massive march in central Paris, adding she hoped Macron would listen.

At Paris’s Place de la Republique, protesters gathered beneath banners demanding better-funded schools, including one reading “Neglected schools, sacrificed youth”.

An AFP reporter described the Paris march as largely peaceful, but tensions flared near its endpoint in the east of the capital as police fired tear gas and some demonstrators threw rocks at a line of officers carrying riot shields.

Police officials said that “300 hostile individuals” attempted to confront officers.

Yanis, 16, said students felt ignored until the demonstrations turned violent. “It makes us feel like everything gets solved through violence,” he said.

The unrest comes ahead of a 2027 election to choose Macron’s successor, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls despite a graft conviction.

While many protests have been peaceful, some demonstrators have started fires, destroyed bus shelters or clashed with riot police.

Police have responded with batons, tear gas and riot-control rounds.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu condemned violence linked to the protests, telling lawmakers the violence would not be tolerated.

“Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings,” he told parliament, rejecting accusations that the government had ordered “police repression” against protesters.

He also said that high schools across the country would be closed for a half-day between Wednesday and Friday, to permit “internal democracy” in the establishments.

The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start of the movement.

The government has sought to address the students’ grievances, while accusing the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of encouraging the movement.

Veteran LFI presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has strongly supported the protests, while calling for non-violent methods.

Thousands of arrests

Thomas, a 17-year-old student from the Paris suburb of Val-de-Marne, said some of the classrooms at his school were short of desks and chairs while the bathrooms lacked doors, toilet paper and soap.

“We just want better conditions for studying,” he told AFP. Teachers and parents joined demonstrations across France.

In Lyon, parents organised to support the youngsters, while teacher Rindala Younes said she wanted to help students “convey their message peacefully”.

“The high school students’ demands are legitimate,” she said.

In neighbouring Belgium, students have started a similar protest movement in the city of Liege. On Tuesday, several of them were arrested after what police said were clashes and vandalism on the sidelines of a demonstration.

news.title: Brazil Battle
news.text:
Brazil, the largest South American country with a Leftist government, is poised to come within the orbit of the influence of US President Donald Trump as Flavio Bolsonaro, son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro, finished ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the election on 4 October, which will go to a run-off in three weeks. The surprise result proved wrong opinion poll projections that had shown President Lula in the lead. Flavio Bolsonaro got 47% of votes against the incumbent’s 45%. If Bolsonaro continues his winning streak in the October 25 election, Brazil will be the latest country to swing to the right in Latin America. The result has caused a shock to Lula who at 81 is seeking a fourth term in office. The veteran leftist had earlier called the vote a battle between democracy and “barbarism,” warning voters that Brazil’s sovereignty was in danger in the face of US pressure. Irony is Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, was little known nationally before his jailed father made him his political heir. He had never expressed ambition to follow in his father’s footsteps.

However, it has so turned out that his father’s powerful name virtually performed a miracle and the country’s conservative vote bank rallied behind the son, despite a campaign marked by scandals and mudslinging. In fact, during the campaign itself Flavio was under investigation for corruption over financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father. But apparently it did not cut much ice with many voters. This is a remarkable fightback for the Bolsonaro family after Jair Bolsonaro lost a re-election bid in 2022 that led to violent riots in the capital and his conviction last year for attempting a coup. He is serving a sentence of 27 years in jail. His son has already announced that if he becomes President, he will appoint four new judges to the powerful Supreme Court that convicted his father and try to overturn the verdict. It has been Trump’s policy to ensure one Latin American country after another elects candidates he backs as Presidents. He had said he was watching the election in Brazil “very closely.” He has wielded tariffs and sanctions to corner Lula for the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro and alleged unfair trade practices. Lula repeatedly warned him not to “meddle” in the elections. Lula had endeared himself to his countrymen for social welfare programmes that lifted many out of poverty. He made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after being jailed on a corruption conviction for 18 months. The charges, thrown out on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him. In his third term, he managed the economy well, causing a drop in inflation and unemployment.

However, voters were seemingly unhappy with him for a high cost of living and a continuing spiral of crime and violence. In Brazil, the number one issue for voters is safety as there is a perception that security has worsened. Other reasons, experts point out, are persisting inequalities and a lack of access to land, markets and opportunities. If Flavio wins the race in the run-off elections, where only two candidates – he and Lula – will be allowed to contest, his main task will be to persuade Trump to ease high tariffs imposed on Brazil under Lula. Trump’s actions have hurt the Brazilian economy and that indirectly damages Lula’s chances of re-election. But being a close ally of the US does not automatically mean getting better treatment. There are chances Trump may treat Flavio with disrespect, as he has treated other allied governments earlier. A Lula win would leave Brazil among a shrinking group of Latin American countries standing up to Trump. If he loses, only Mexico and Uruguay will be the bigger countries left to take on the US.

news.title: Fact Check: Do Vaccines Contain Nanotechnology That Can Control Humans?
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Content claiming that vaccination can control humans and turn them into zombies has been circulating on Facebook via two accounts; account one [archive] and two since August 2026.The first post includes a video of US President Donald Trump announcing an energy policy based on artificial intelligence. The launch of this technology is linked to a narrative about implanting nanotechnology via vaccine injections to control humans.“Many people will enter an irreversible state and become zombies—half-human, half-machine—because ‘nanotechnology’ is injected into the bloodstream.”Do vaccines really contain nanotechnology that controls humans?FACT CHECKTempo verified this content through a reverse image search and expert interviews. The findings show that no type of vaccine can turn humans into zombies. This conspiracy theory is an old narrative that has been circulating since the COVID-19 pandemic.Video VerificationThe video clip used in the post originates from broadcasts by the "LiveNOW from Fox" YouTube channel and the Fox Business Facebook account on July 24, 2026. In the original video, US President Donald Trump announced a policy supporting the construction of power plants for artificial intelligence (AI)-based technology companies.Trump stated that the policy aims to maintain electricity access for residents, meet industrial needs, and provide added value to the community. He emphasized that the rapid development of artificial intelligence and the surge in energy demand are inevitable realities that society must keep pace with.Vaccines Are Not Tools for ControlAirlangga University (Unair) virologist Arif Ansori emphasizes that vaccines do not contain nanochips capable of being activated by 5G or 6G signals, or by artificial intelligence technology. Individuals who have received the vaccine cannot be controlled or transformed into zombies.“Vaccination cannot control human thoughts or behavior, nor can it take over the human body,” Arif told Tempo via WhatsApp message on Wednesday, September 30, 2026.Arif explained that immunization aims to stimulate the formation of an adaptive immune response and immunological memory. This mechanism prepares the immune system to respond more rapidly upon exposure to the actual pathogen.“Vaccines work by introducing antigens—or biological information that enables the immune system to recognize specific antigens—to the body,” he said.Vaccines do not replace the immune system; instead, they harness the natural mechanisms of adaptive immunity to generate specific B cells, antibodies, T cells, and memory cells.The vaccine production process is strictly supervised by the National Agency of Drug and Food Control (BPOM) to ensure quality, safety, and efficacy prior to distribution. This oversight continues even as the vaccines are administered to the public.Aji Muhawarman, Head of the Bureau of Communication and Public Information at the Ministry of Health, stated that vaccination aims to generate specific antibodies so that individuals do not suffer severe illness upon infection by pathogens.“Immunization is one way to provide active immunity that complements the body's natural immunity,” Aji told Tempo on Friday, October 2, 2026.Origin of the NarrativeThe claim that vaccination turns humans into zombies originated with Pierre Gilbert, a Canadian speaker and conspiracy theorist, in 1996. At the time, Gilbert stated that humans would turn into zombies due to vaccination in the year 2000, leading up to the apocalypse.That narrative resurfaced during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. However, the administration of billions of COVID-19 vaccine doses worldwide proved the claim to be entirely unfounded.Gilbert himself is a practitioner of alternative medicine, including chiropractic, acupuncture, and naturopathy. He describes himself as a follower of eschatology—a branch of theology that studies the end times based on specific religious doctrines.CONCLUSIONTempo's verification concludes that the narrative claiming vaccines aim to control minds and turn humans into zombies is false.**Do you have information or claims that you want to have fact-checked? Contact our ChatBot. You can also send criticism, objections, or feedback for this Fact-Checking article via email to cekfakta@tempo.co.id.
news.summary: Fact Check - Vaccines do not contain nanotechnology that can control humans or turn them into zombies.

news.title: Donald Trump Reiterates Claims On Hormuz, Says Waterway Belongs to US, Its Navy
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has reiterated his claim that the Strait of Hormuz is under US control, saying the strategic waterway “belongs to the United States of America” and its Navy. Trump also warned that Iranian vessels attempting to breach the US naval blockade could be sunk, further escalating his rhetoric over the key maritime route.

The comments came as Washington continues its military and economic pressure on Tehran amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict. Trump has repeatedly asserted that the US Navy controls maritime traffic through the Strait and has described the American naval presence as a blockade. Iran Offers To Reopen Strait of Hormuz Within 7 Days if US Eases Military Pressure and Lifts Port Blockade.

Trump Says Strait of Hormuz ‘Belongs’ to US

Speaking to reporters, Trump said the Strait of Hormuz “belongs to the United States of America” while discussing the US naval blockade and the movement of oil through the waterway.

Trump also described how Iranian vessels attempting to circumvent the blockade could be dealt with, saying ships carrying oil could be targeted and that vessels without oil could be sunk.

The remarks mark another strong statement from Trump over the strategic waterway, after he previously claimed that the US had “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump Warns Iranian Ships Against Breaching Blockade

Trump said the US would continue enforcing restrictions on Iranian shipping through the Strait. His comments come as Washington maintains a significant naval presence in the region and seeks to restrict Iran's ability to move oil through the key maritime corridor. The Strait of Hormuz is Spilling Oil into the Persian Gulf.

The US president has previously said that only vessels permitted by American forces would be allowed to pass through the waterway. The White House has also described US naval control of the Strait as part of its broader pressure campaign against Iran.

Strait of Hormuz Remains Key Flashpoint in US-Iran War

The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and is one of the world's most important energy shipping routes. Disruptions in the waterway can have significant consequences for global oil supplies and prices.

The conflict has already affected energy flows through the Strait. Reuters reported that the waterway normally handles roughly one-fifth of global oil shipments, making continued disruption a major concern for international energy markets.

Recent reporting has indicated that oil flows have recovered from earlier levels, although shipping through the Strait remains dependent on US military operations and continues to face security risks.

Iran Has Rejected US Claims of Control

Iran has previously rejected Trump's assertions that Washington has full control over the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran has maintained that US statements do not alter the status of the waterway and has linked any reopening of the route to its own conditions.

Trump's latest comments therefore add to an already tense dispute over who controls maritime movement through the strategically important passage.

US Military Presence in Region

The United States has expanded its military presence around Iran during the conflict. Recent reports indicate that additional US naval forces, including aircraft carriers and amphibious groups, are being deployed in the region, potentially adding thousands of personnel.

Trump's latest remarks come amid continuing uncertainty over the future of the US-Iran conflict and negotiations surrounding the Strait. He has previously indicated that the conflict could end through negotiations or further military action if an agreement is not reached.

news.title: Must-Win Republican Candidate Brutally Snubs Trump on Debate Stage
news.text:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins has given President Donald Trump the cold shoulder during a televised debate that could make or break her re-election hopes.

Collins, a vulnerable five-term senator from Maine, was asked if she would welcome Trump to campaign alongside her—a question that comes on the heels of Trump telling reporters Monday that he is considering traveling to Maine to campaign.

Collins awkwardly answered: “I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine. He’s talking about going to a lot of different, uh, states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite, uhh, senator, I—” 

“So yes or no?” Lagerquist interrupted. “Do you have a yes or no to that?”

Collins once again skirted the straightforward question by repeating her refrain. 

“I would say that he is not coming to Maine,” she said. 

As Collins, 73, struggled with her answer, her opponent, Troy Jackson, a 58-year-old logger and former Maine Senate president, shook his head in exasperation. 

Trump has been crisscrossing several states in a frantic campaign push as Republicans are poised for a disastrous Election Day. Multiple Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from Trump, whose approval rating continues to fall as war rages on with Iran and prices remain sky-high at the pump. 

Trump teased a possible trip to Collins’ backyard on Monday, saying, “I think we’re going to Maine, too.”

The White House and Collins’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

Collins’ Trump snub comes as the president’s standing remains underwater in Maine, where 40 percent of registered voters approve of his job performance compared to 59 percent who disapprove, according to a Marist poll from this month. The same survey found Collins on the brink of losing her Senate seat after nearly 30 years in power, trailing Jackson by four points.

Collins, who has spent years walking a political tightrope in purple Maine—occasionally breaking with Trump without losing his backing—repeatedly highlighted how she has pushed back on the president’s unpopular policies, like tariffs, during the debate. 

But Jackson pounced on her history of siding with Trump, delivering a stinging line after Collins noted that she voted against the final passage of Trump’s “Big, Beautiful Bill”—after voting to advance it in the Senate. 

“Senator Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.”

news.title: Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: 5 takeaways from Maine Senate debate
news.text:
Five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson clashed over President Donald Trump and their records in the first debate for the Maine U.S. Senate seat that could decide which party takes power in Washington.

The race is being closely watched nationally as it could determine control of the Senate, which is narrowly held by Republicans, 53-47. Recent polls have shown a tight race: a University of New Hampshire poll from mid-September found Jackson ahead by 4 percentage points, while a New York Times/Siena University poll from a similar time period found Collins ahead by 3 percentage points.

It’s also been a race mired in scandal. Jackson, the former Maine Senate President, replaced oyster farmer Graham Platner as the Democratic nominee in July following a sexual assault allegation that Platner denies. Collins and Jackson have also both faced accusations of misconduct against their campaigns in recent weeks.

The candidates responded to these accusations and discussed a wide range of issues, from affordability to their records to Trump, in the debate broadcast on WGME. Here are five takeaways.

The Trump issue

Jackson sought to tie Collins to Trump throughout the debate, repeatedly saying that Collins has voted with Trump 96% of the time and that her Republican colleagues have called her a “team player.” He criticized Collins for advancing the One Big Beautiful Bill out of committee, voting to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court and voting for a $70 billion funding package for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Collins, on the other hand, tried to distance herself from the president. She argued that the 96% is too high and based on only one study, while another found her voting with Trump only 72% of the time. She said that she has consistently voted against her party and that she ultimately voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill. She also highlighted other areas where she has broken with Trump, such as voting to end the war in Iran and against the tariffs in Canada.

Collins has long had a reputation as a moderate Republican, but it's been difficult to thread the needle in the Trump era. The president has floated a visit to Maine, and when asked if she would "stand with him" if he does, she didn’t give a yes or no answer.

“I don't think that President Trump is going to come to Maine. He's talking about going to a lot of different states,” Collins said. “I've heard nothing from his office, and I'm not exactly his favorite senator.”

Bringing home the bacon

Collins has long been known as someone who “brings home the bacon” to Maine, a term that means she secures federal dollars for her state. She brought it up immediately in her opening statement.

“In the past four years, I've secured $1.5 billion for 672 projects, from Madawaska to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford,” Collins said.

She also frequently cited specific policies she helped author, like a $50 billion fund to help rural healthcare and the Paycheck Protection Program, which she said saved 250,000 jobs in Maine.

This strategy of “pork barrel politics” and specific policy details is a time-honored one among incumbent politicians, but it has lately fallen by the wayside as newcomers campaign in more flashy ways. Collins may be hoping that emphasizing her loyalty to Maine will help her to overcome national headwinds against Republicans.

However, Jackson argued that the money she brings back pales in comparison to the money lost by Trump’s policies. He said that Collins “is like an arsonist who helps set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out."

Jackson said he made sure to pass progressive policies in the state Senate like lowering prescription drug and universal school meals, although he provided limited details on specific legislation. 

Who will get stuff done?

Similarly, Collins stressed her bipartisanship and ability to get things done in Congress, areas where she said Jackson might struggle. She attacked him for not being able to get bills passed when serving in the state house.

“How do you think you’re going to get things done in a mostly divided Senate as the most junior senator?” she asked. “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships.”

Jackson responded that Collins doesn’t understand the legislative process in Maine and that some bills must be discarded to make progress. He suggested that what she is getting passed isn't aligned with Mainer's priorities.

“Senator Collins is saying that she's been passing more bills in Congress. I mean, I don't see it,” Jackson said. “I certainly don't think that, you know, a lot of the ones that she has been fighting for has been helping us.”

Collins and Jackson respond to scandals

Collins and Jackson have faced various accusations in recent weeks. On Sept. 22, ProPublica reported that the FBI had ended an investigation into allegations that a fundraiser for Collins had participated in an illegal campaign donation scheme after the Trump administration purged the Justice Department and FBI of its teams that handle public corruption cases.

Collins called the allegations “completely false” and “very offensive.”

Jackson has faced an attack from a GOP ad that accuses him of abusing his power when he was state Senate president to help out his lobbyist son. Jackson said that independent fact checkers have proved “that there was nothing there.”

Collins also attacked Jackson for claiming a Federal Housing Authority loan on his Allagash home, which he claimed was his primary residence when he was living part-time in Augusta as state Senate president. However, the Maine Ethics Commission voted against investigating Jackson at the time, saying he had not violated campaign finance law.

Whose fault is it — Washington's or Maine's?

Both candidates agreed that families are struggling in Maine. But they disagreed on the cause. Collins argued that Maine’s high electricity rates, housing costs and property taxes are due to failures at the state house level, while Jackson blamed policies passed under the Trump administration in Washington, including the Iran war and the One Big Beautiful Bill.

news.title: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran ‘take out’ LA and San Diego
news.text:

Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.

While speaking in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, he said: “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego.”

There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.

San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his “reckless war talk”.

In a second post on his official governor of California X account, Newsom shared an article on the comments from the Los Angeles Times saying it was “disgusting and disqualifying”.

Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California’s leaders.

news.title: WHO Assesses Low Plague Risk in Russia After New Case Reports
news.text:
A reported death of a laboratory technician in Siberia that sparked fears of plague has prompted the World Health Organization to issue a measured assessment, saying the overall public health risk in Russia appears low.

Concern flared after reports claimed pneumonic plague had killed 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked at an anti-plague institute in the Irkutsk region. The allegation drew attention because the area is known for naturally occurring plague among wild animals.

“The WHO initial risk assessment from the information available estimates the risk to be moderate to low for Irkutsk, a low risk for the Russian Federation as a whole, and very low for the WHO European region,” UN health agency spokesman Christian Lindmeier said.

Speaking at a press briefing in Geneva, Mr Lindmeier said: “A woman who worked at a laboratory in Irkutsk oblast has died, and the authorities are looking into whether pneumonic plague caused her death.”

He said Ms Shipilova had been employed at a facility that researches dangerous pathogens in Siberia, where plague circulates in wildlife, underscoring why local authorities were treating the case with caution.

“The illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection,” he said.

Mr Lindmeier added that officials had traced and identified people who had been in contact with her and put them under observation.

“According to the test results, no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts,” he said.

He said the agency was continuing to track developments. “WHO is following the situation closely, working with headquarters to keep other countries informed,” and it is prepared to assist Russian authorities if requested.

Moscow has moved to play down claims that Ms Shipilova died of plague, even as US President Donald Trump said the United States was monitoring the reports and stood ready to offer support.

“We’re looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it,” Mr Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington planned to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.

“We’ll help them, we’ll help them as much as we can.”

The Russian outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, reported that Ms Shipilova may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.

Other outlets also pointed to a possible connection between her death and a laboratory accident at the institute.

People of Baikal said as many as 200 people who may have had contact with her were under quarantine, but did not provide further details.

Russian officials, however, emphasised that post-mortem testing had not found evidence of the disease.

Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said an inspection by a special expert commission concluded that “the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology”.

In a message posted on Telegram, he said tests conducted by Russia’s consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor found that “no microorganisms linked to the young woman’s professional work were found in her biological samples”.

He also said there had been “no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention” since her death.

Mr Kobzev described the sanitary-epidemiological situation in Irkutsk as “stable”.

“The situation remains under our control and that of the experts.”

‘Rumours and speculations’

When questioned yesterday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged reporters to “rely on Rospotrebnadzor’s official statements rather than … rumours and speculations”.

Plague is a bacterial disease that can emerge in several forms. Pneumonic plague is the most contagious and can spread via respiratory transmission, while bubonic plague is typically spread through infected fleas.

According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early.

The developments are being followed closely in Washington, where the Covid-19 pandemic, which began during Mr Trump’s first term, remains a defining reference point for health security fears.

Mr Trump has repeatedly endorsed the theory that Covid-19 resulted from a laboratory leak in Wuhan, China.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States was tracking the situation in Russia but saw no “cause for alarm”.

“There’s very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously, but like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread,” Mr Rubio told reporters before departing for a visit to Iceland.

“So we’re watching and monitoring it closely. I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it. And we’re doing that.”

Experts said the measures reported so far in Russia appeared “proportionate”.

“It appears that measures are being implemented to quarantine any potential contacts and prevent any onward transmission,” Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology at Imperial College London, said in a commentary.

news.title: Islam Wanting to Take Over: Trump Blames France Protests on Migration
news.text: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday blamed France's mass student protests on Islam and migration, pushing his global right-wing narrative ahead of tough midterm elections at home. "What's happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social network. "This isn't about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" French students have blocked the entrances to hundreds of high schools across the country since late September to demand better conditions, in protests that have descended into sporadic clashes with security forces. A quarter of a million demonstrators took to the streets across France on Tuesday. Trump did not elaborate on his claims or provide any evidence. In France, no link has yet been established between the student movement and any religious or identity-based demands. But leading voices in Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement have been using the French protests to ram home points about immigration ahead of the US midterm elections next month. MAGA commentators repeatedly posted videos of the French unrest in the days leading up to Trump's post. "The riots in France are a clear warning to the rest of the West," Trump ally Glenn Beck said on X on Monday. "What is happening in France today is all part of an international network of socialists working to dismantle the West." "This will come to America if the Democrats take power again," posted right-wing commentator Dave Rubin to his 1.6 million followers, along with footage filmed in a French train station. - 'Civilizational erasure' - Trump, 80, has ramped up his rhetoric on core issues like migration and transgender people ahead of the midterms, as the Iran war and the cost of living look set to cost Republicans control of Congress. At the same time, Europe has been a target for Trump ever since his first term in the White House. And his second administration has been keener than ever to warn of what it calls the decline of Western culture on the other side of the Atlantic. The US national security strategy released in December said Europe faced "civilizational erasure" -- and in extraordinary language towards close allies, said it would be "cultivating resistance" to current political trends. Vice President JD Vance has also been a vocal critic of Europe on the same issue. Even Trump's handshake-heavy "bromance" with outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron has failed to keep the US leader from criticizing a key ally. But France responded to Trump's reaction by comparing it to that of Iran, which earlier summoned the French envoy over what it called Paris's "violent response" to the school protests. "You'll get the Iranians' version, perhaps the version from some Israelis, perhaps the version from some Americans," France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told a parliamentary committee on Tuesday. Barrot said French diplomatic missions were trying to put across the French case "so that we have our own narratives to disseminate, rather than being subjected to those of others."

news.title: Trump says call scheduled with Putin to discuss possible plague death in Russia
news.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute. 

Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said he would be talking with Putin about the case "very soon." Health authorities are investigating after the death of an employee at an anti-plague institute, which authorities attributed to pneumonia with an unknown cause.

Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in "very deep discussions" on the topic. "We'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow," Trump said.

The World Health Organization on Tuesday said the case presents a "very low" risk outside Russia. The United Nations agency said it was in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. 

On Monday, Trump said the U.S. would be willing to help Russia with the situation. 

The call also comes as the Trump administration faces an Oct. 18 deadline to decide which Russian entities, if any, it will sanction under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.

Ukraine has given the administration and Congress a wish list of Russian companies, vessels and individuals it would like to see hit with U.S. sanctions under that law.
news.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.

news.title: RAF Fairford Base Threat Aimed To Kill US Troops and Destroy Military Aircraft, Says Official
news.text:
A US-run military air base in England faced Iranian-related threats and the Trump administration believed the intention was to kill as many American troops and destroy as many US planes as possible, a US official said. The official, who was not authorised to comment publicly on the matter and spoke on condition of anonymity, could not speak to the nature of the potential attack. The United States removed its bombers from RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, which has been used by American planes to strike Iran during this year’s war.

The new details come as British police on Tuesday arrested a 22-year-old British man in central London on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, reported. He is the seventh person arrested in connection with the suspected plot, which authorities have linked to Iran, but police so far have released few details of their investigation. US Evacuates Dozen B-1 Bombers From UK’s RAF Fairford Airbase Over Suspected Iranian Threat.

London Arrest Marks Seventh Detention in Widening Counterterrorism Probe

The central London arrest follows a series of detentions carried out over the past ten days across England. Five British men in their 20s were detained near the perimeter of the base in the early hours of Sept. 27, and a 25-year-old British Iranian man was arrested in London on Thursday. All six were released on bail while under investigation.

Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said detectives “remain committed to investigating all possible angles.” UK PM Andy Burnham ‘Strong Indications’ Iran Involved in RAF Fairford Security Incident.

“We’re acutely aware of the public interest in this investigation, and we are working around the clock, and at pace, to identify the motivation behind events in Gloucestershire,” she said.

Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swooped on the rural area late at night. Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant, gasoline, in three vans linked to the five suspects, but no explosives.

Strategic Bombers Redeployed to United States Amid Security Fears

The United States moved its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, and the Pentagon said all American bombers at the facility had been redeployed to their home bases in the US

US President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he didn’t want to tempt “the enemy” by having the bombers there.

“We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” he said in Washington. He said that the people who made the threat “would be linked to Iran,” but he didn’t offer details.

British officials have declined to comment on reports that the bombers were moved because of fears of a drone attack on the base. The prime minister’s spokesman, Tom Wells, said Monday he was “not going to comment on foreign nations’ military operations.” But he insisted that RAF Fairford is safe.

Transatlantic Diplomatic and Regional Friction

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the United Kingdom saw “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without saying why or what the nature of the suspected plot was. Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

The UK-owned base has been used by American B-1 and B-52 bombers during the Iran war. The British government allowed the US military to use RAF Fairford for what it called defensive strikes on Iranian missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on UK interests and Britain’s allies in the Gulf.

The mysterious incident near the base came at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on UK soil. British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025.

UK officials also say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arsons and other attacks in the UK and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the UK if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

The disclosure comes as British counterterrorism police arrested a 22-year-old man in central London on Tuesday, marking the seventh arrest tied to the investigation in Gloucestershire.

news.title: Trump reveals the make of his suit – and it isn’t what people were expecting
news.text:
President Donald Trump has revealed the make of his suit — and it’s not the luxury Italian label he’s known for wearing. 

At a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Monday night, Trump was photographed pulling back his Navy suit jacket to reveal the company behind his signature attire. 

A tag sewn into the jacket lining read, “Jos. A. Bank,” which markets its “everyday low prices” on its website. People on social media noted the detour from the Brioni suits the president’s worn since the days of his 2000s reality show, The Apprentice. 

“Common wisdom has long been that Trump only wears Brioni suits (Brioni supplied him with wardrobe for The Apprentice), but lately he’s been wearing this navy Jos A Bank suit,” Aidan McLaughlin, Washington correspondent for Vanity Fair, wrote on X Tuesday. 

Trump said in his 2004 book, Think Like a Billionaire, that Brioni provided him with suits for his reality show. “I wear Brioni suits, which I buy off the rack,” Trump wrote, per a New York Times article published in 2016 about the-then first time presidential candidate’s fashion sense. 

In the article, Hope Hicks, Trump’s campaign spokeswoman at the time, said he was wearing Brioni in the lead-up to the 2016 election, but that he also likes other suit makers, including the Brooklyn label Martin Greenfield Clothiers. 

A suit from Jos. A. Bank typically ranges from $250 to $580, while a suit from Brioni can range from $5,500 to $16,200. But money isn’t likely an object for Trump, whose financial disclosures reportedly reveal that he made at least $2.2 billion last year.

The Independent has reached out to the White House for comment on Trump’s suit choices. 

People online also pointed out that Trump, known for pushing companies to build more facilities in the U.S., opted for a label that offshores most of its manufacturing. 

Menswear writer Derek Guy shared on X, “Interesting. Jos. A. Bank suits are all made overseas, typically in countries like China and Bangladesh. 

“They carry an associate label called Joseph Abboud, which is made in the United States. I wonder why Trump chose the cheap import over the US-made suit.”

Democratic communicator Josh Dorner wrote, “In the middle of HIS massive trade war, Trump shows off the label of a suit made…not in America.”

Shortly into his second term, Trump announced sweeping tariffs against adversaries and allies, claiming their trade policies were unfair toward Americans. Most of the tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court in February, which ruled that the global levies were unlawfully imposed.
news.summary: The president has worn Brioni suits since the days of his reality show, ‘The Apprentice’

news.title: Fuel industry warns truck stops not to sell red dye diesel after Trump lifts restrictions
news.text:
Truck stops nationwide were warned to “proceed with caution” Tuesday by a major industry group after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to promote the use of “red dye” diesel fuel.

Red dye diesel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farm equipment and other off-road uses.

The order, signed before farmers in Nebraska on Monday night, aims to bring down fuel prices by “temporarily” allowing highway use of red dye diesel fuel, according to a White House statement. 

U.S. voters are deeply frustrated by the high price of gas, and the Trump administration is under intense pressure to bring down fuel costs before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Monday’s order instructs Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to “defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations and to provide penalty relief to the extent permitted by law.” 

It does not waive the federal taxes, because only Congress can eliminate a tax.

Following Trump’s directive, the Energy Marketers of America warned gas stations to “proceed with caution.”

“Whether relief is available, whom it covers, and on what conditions depend on Treasury determinations and guidance not yet issued,” the group said. “Deferral is not forgiveness.”

Moreover, the order does not “resolve EPA or state restrictions” on the dyed variety of diesel fuel, the EMA said. 

Other trucking and gas industry groups sounded a similar note of caution.

“The White House appears to be trying to encourage the supply chain to move toward selling dyed fuel in non-traditional ways,” the Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of America and the National Association of Truck Stop Owners said in a note to their members.

“We do not expect most reputable diesel retailers and fuel marketers to do this,” they said. “First, the tax is still owed, so there’s limited upside.” 

In addition, “the logistical challenges outweigh any visible upside: Residual dye lingers in tanks and fuel systems.”

For most fuel sellers, “the liability and customer risk outweigh any temporary, uncertain benefit.”

The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment. 

A group representing independent long-haul truckers also suggested Trump’s move would provide little benefit to its members.

“Allowing the wider use of red-dyed diesel will provide minimal relief. Market stability is essential to bring down costs for the long haul,” said Todd Spencer, president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association.

Since the war with Iran began, the price of diesel has surged from $3.76 per gallon to $6.32 as of Tuesday, a nearly 70% increase.

The Iran conflict is not the only conflict contributing to diesel’s skyrocketing price. 

A recent escalation of the Ukraine-Russia war has included strikes by Ukrainian drones on Russian refineries. 

Russia, traditionally one of the world’s large diesel exporters, has responded to the attacks by imposing a diesel export ban through at least the end of October.

Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russia’s diesel infrastructure.

“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters in early September. “There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”

Oil prices also remain sharply elevated since the beginning of the year. Brent crude oil, which traded Tuesday night above $101 per barrel, is up more than 66% since the start of the year.

news.title: Putin pal responds to Trump’s claim that Don Jr. paid him back for wedding
news.text:
Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev said Tuesday that Donald Trump Jr. had reimbursed him for funding a portion of his recent Bahamas wedding celebration, though Kremlev questioned why the repayment was made.

“Yes, he did,” Kremlev said during an International Boxing Association press conference in Istanbul. “He did repay the money I spent on the present.”

Neither Kremlev nor the Trump family provided proof that any money was actually repaid.

Kremlev, who heads the boxing association and was recently awarded the Order of Friendship by Russian President Vladimir Putin, expressed confusion over the transaction.

“Frankly speaking, I do not understand why he decided to do so,” he said through an interpreter. “There are all kinds of events organized by all kinds of people. It is as if I invite you to come and visit my country house. Would you expect me to issue an invoice to them afterward?”

He added that doing so would be “ridiculous.”

Kremlev helped bankroll Trump Jr.’s three-day luxury wedding in the Bahamas when the president’s eldest son married socialite Bettina Anderson in May. 

According to records reviewed by ProPublica, Kremlev footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars in expenses, including renting one of two private islands where a reception was held and guests stayed, as well as an elaborate fireworks display. The money reportedly came from an entity tied to the International Boxing Association in Dubai, which is used by the organization to conduct financial transactions.

Following the initial report, President Donald Trump defended his son, telling reporters that while the financial support was “totally allowed,” the funds would be returned.

“It’s totally allowed,” Trump said. “But, as I understand it, he paid them back.” 

He added: “That’s very common. I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people.” 

Bettina Trump previously addressed the reporting in an Instagram post signed by the couple, writing that they were married “surrounded ONLY by our family.” 

She described Kremlev as a “dear friend” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding.” 

Last month, the White House directed The Independent to her post, where she had written: “Apparently our wedding is making headlines again, so a little clarity seems in order. ... It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.” 

Kremlev dismissed the scrutiny surrounding the event, describing the gathering as “a shared event” and stating that “people blew it out of proportion.”

“I mean, why can’t we be friends?” Kremlev said. “We are just friends. We are simply friends and what unites us is love for sports.”

Born Umar Lutfuloyev, Kremlev served criminal convictions for extortion and battery in his 20s before changing his name and rising through Russian sports administration with backing from top security officials. 

Since taking control of the International Boxing Association in 2020, he moved key operations to Russia, relied on Russian state-energy giant Gazprom for funding, and oversaw the International Olympic Committee stripping the boxing organization of its official recognition in 2023 over governance concerns. 

Kremlev and Trump Jr. have maintained a public connection, hosting a sports event together in September 2025 where Trump Jr. called him “not only a leader but a friend.” Kremlev’s press office told ProPublica the two share a friendly relationship but have never discussed political matters.

The focus comes amid Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine following its 2022 invasion, and follows previous attention on Trump Jr.’s contacts with Russian figures. 

During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump Jr. drew criticism for a meeting with a Russian attorney at Trump Tower regarding potential campaign information about his father’s opponent, which became a key point in subsequent inquiries into Russian election interference.

news.title: Firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan scheduled for December
news.text:
The acting secretary of the U.S. Army said Tuesday that the man convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.

In a post on social media, acting Secretary Adam Telle said the execution of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan will take place at Fort Hood.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan. The U.S. military has not carried out the death penalty since 1961. 

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting medical checkups, shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed and more than 30 injured.

He said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims and made almost no effort to defend himself at trial. He told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”

Trump’s approval triggered a series of procedural steps toward carrying out the execution, but Hasan could put them on hold — potentially for years — with a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.
news.summary: The acting secretary of the U.S. Army says the man convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3

news.title: Oil prices rise as storms and air strikes threaten supply
news.text:
PERTH: Oil prices rose on Wednesday as the market weighed supply constraints from a storm heading for US oil-producing regions and attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia against increased supplies of ​Middle East crude.

Brent futures rose 93 cents, or 0.92%, to $101.51 a barrel by 0022 GMT. ‌

US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 82 cents, or 0.92%, to $90.25.

US forecasters said on Tuesday a storm forming in the Gulf of Mexico would become the first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 within two days and would likely hit oil and gas producing facilities.

The offshore ​areas in the Gulf in the storm’s path produce 15% of US crude oil and 5% ​of the country’s natural gas.

KCM Trade chief analyst Tim Waterer said the storm was an “unwelcome ⁠complication for crude, raising the prospect of production and refining disruptions at a time when the market ​already has enough supply-side headaches”.

The storm could affect six refineries.

Refineries in US Gulf states account for about 50% of ​the national capacity of 18.2 million barrels per day (bpd).

US crude oil and gasoline inventories fell, while distillate stocks rose marginally last week, market sources said on Tuesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.

Crude stocks fell by 2.09 million barrels in the week ended ​October 2.

Supply had been rising as the East-West pipeline hit 5.8 million barrels a day, according to Saudi ​Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman on Tuesday.

Around 12 million barrels per day of crude oil and 2 million bpd of ‌refined products ⁠were leaving the Middle East on tankers in the last 7 to 10 days, the head of Vitol said.

However, Saudi Arabia’s airports in Jazan and Najran were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, the Saudi aviation authority said, as hostilities between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis escalated.

The attacks occurred as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces pressed a ​major offensive to retake territory ​from the Houthis, after ⁠weeks of rebel advances, with Riyadh stepping up airstrikes in support of the campaign.

Attacks and refinery outages are “likely to keep the cracks elevated and scarcity will transmit to ​crude. Prices will stay elevated near a $100 level without any material de-escalation emerging,” ​said Mukesh Sahdev, ⁠chief oil analyst at X Analysts in Sydney.

US-Iran relations are no closer to repair with US President Donald Trump saying on Tuesday that nobody knew who was running Iran during the eight-month US-Israeli war with Iran.

“Their leaders are gone, their ⁠second group ​of leaders are gone, and the biggest problem I have is ​nobody knows who the hell is running the country,” Trump said.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman said on Sunday Washington knows very well who their ​counterpart is in Iran and how the decision-making system in Iran works.

news.title: Mother of lab worker who died in suspected plague case says 'They destroyed my daughter'
news.text:
The mother of a Russian lab worker who died after a suspected pneumonic plague infection has spoken out to say authorities ‘let her daughter die.’

Victim Daria Shipilova’s mother, Svetlana, told Russian media she and other family members remain in lockdown so are unable to bury the 28-year-old, reports The Sun.

Svetlana, who is herself a medic, accused those responsible for her daughter’s treatment of ‘abandoning’ her.

She is reported to have said, “I’ve saved plenty of patients, yet they couldn’t save my daughter. They simply let my daughter die.

“I’m waiting for it to become official. It has to be an official document. It’s very hard for me right now. This whole spectacle drags on.”

Russian media reported that Daria died after a test tube broke while she was working in a lab in Irkutsk, Siberia, although her mother disputes this.

She is thought to have been studying bacteria called Yersinia pestis, which killed millions during the Middle Ages.

Daria was reportedly part of an expedition in Buryatia, on Russia’s border with Mongolia – where she studied plague-infested squirrels.

The researcher died of what officials have termed ‘pneumonia of unknown aetiology’.

According to France 24, the governor of the Irkutsk region denied anyone died as a result of working with dangerous pathogens, and there have been few details released over how Daria passed away.

Officials were quick, however, to place several hospitals and almost 200 people into a strict quarantine lockdown after reports of her death.

The World Health Organisation has responded to the death by asking Russia for updates.

US President Donald Trump has offered to help Russia, warning that the plague is ‘stronger and smarter’ than current vaccines.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said America would be “watching and monitoring it closely”.

He said: “There’s very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously.

“But like anything else, something like that gets out and could quickly spread. So we’re watching and monitoring it closely.”

Daria’s mother insisted her daughter would not have broken a test tube.

“Only an amateur would say something like that,” she said.

“It’s simply impossible to spill or break it. They are so heavily protected.”

Asked about the lack of a funeral, she said: “Who is going to bury her if we are sitting here imprisoned?

“She was such a hard worker. A pure, truly pure soul. It is very difficult to get a job there at Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute.

“They destroyed my daughter – abandoned her and destroyed her.”
news.summary: Daria's mother disputes the Russian account of how her daughter died, insisting she was 'no amateur'

news.title: Flying Scared: The Evacuation Of US Bombers From RAF Fairford
news.text:
The evacuation of a dozen B-1B bombers of the US Air
Force from the RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire is another
instalment in the latest rippling of the Iran war that began
as a pre-emptive, illegal assault by the US and Israel on
the Islamic Republic in late February. This, arguably, came
in two parts, the first scripted with the detention and
arrest of five men on September 27 in the vicinity of the
base on suspicion of committing offences under the
Explosives Act and suspicion of preparation of a terrorist
act. (Another was arrested on October 1.) All were British
nationals based in London and speedily released on police
bail. At the time, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor,
head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), floated the suggestion
that “this may be activity committed by proxies, or
individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on
behalf of a foreign state.” The dust had barely settled
before the finger
pointing at Iran began. The men in question, according
to the police, remained under investigation, with their
release “subject to stringent conditions on their movement
and contact with others”.

On October 4, the Pentagon

that “all bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have
been re-deployed to their home stations in the United
States.” The department, wishing to blunt the significance
of this hasty decision, added that the US military bomber
force of B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s remained “ready to deliver
precious global strike capabilities – including through
operations that launch and recover from the continental
United States.”

Two days later, Counter Terrorism
Policing announced
that a further arrest had been made of a dual UK-Iranian man
regarding “activity that took place close to RAF
Fairford.” The arrest was made “on suspicion of
terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006.”
The Senior National Coordinator for CTP, Vicki Evans, reiterated
the line that this remained “a live investigation and our
specialist teams continue to pursue multiple lines of
enquiry into the circumstances surrounding events near RAF

When asked about whether the movement of
the bombers was linked to the September 27 incident, US
Secretary of State Marco Rubio proved
platitudinous and undetailed. “It’s not unusual to see
movement of assets to different parts of the world based on
exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people
coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out.”
This front of airy meaninglessness did not take long to
vanish. The US Vice President JD Vance added salt to the
otherwise dull mix in stating
that the bombers had exited the base out of an “abundance
of caution”. It was felt that Iran was doing what it had
“done for 49 years… which is to engage in acts of
terrorism against the US and against a lot of other

President Donald Trump, tongue ever
loosened, also told
reporters when asked if the bomber redeployment had
arisen from any “specific threat” did not hesitate:
“Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by
accident.” What followed was the usual combination of
adulterated facts and twisted tales. There had been “some
threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we’ll capture
the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them
there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very
far.” Never one to accept the premise that the US security
establishment might err on occasion, the president
reiterated the familiar, if long fossilized line: Washington
“actually knows the people that made the

This dramatic decision to move the bombers
from a base that hosts the US Air Force’s 501st Combat
Support Wing, an important component in the illegal war
against Iran, is very much the opposite of what was
initially done when a farmer noted
the presence of three white vans and a “large group of
hooded and masked men” who then attempted to alert the
Ministry of Defence police at the airbase. When no response
was forthcoming, she made a 999 call to police at 01:36 BST.
Within 10 minutes “the village was full of armed
police.” She ruminated on the effect of the call: “I
believe that my 999 call foiled whatever plans they had.”
She was also “absolutely staggered that it was left to me,
as a member of the public, to see and report this.” The UK
Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, despite thanking
the farmer for her call, suggested she only had “a partial
picture” of what was unfolding, while Trump, claimed
that the men were placed under surveillance “for a long
time, and we got them.”

The swift relocation of such
costly, vulnerable military hardware in the face of a threat
that would, if inflicted, have cost a fraction of any
budget, is also a startling reminder of the turns in modern
warfare. The Ukrainians demonstrated with formidable
efficacy in Operation Spider’s Web how its drones could
strike Russian nuclear-capable bombers, allegedly crippling
a third of its capacity. Taking place in June last year, it

the use of 117 modestly priced drones that had been smuggled
into Russia via lorries by unwitting drivers. The strikes,
taking place across five different time zones with the
assistance of the commercial autopilot software ArduPilot
and the use of artificial intelligence for targeting
purposes, led to an estimated
bill amounting to US$7 billion. Some 41 planes were
damaged or destroyed.

Operation Spider’s Web drew swooning
praise from the cognoscenti. Katja Bego of Chatham House

it “offered a glimpse into the future of warfare,
transformed by access to cheap, widely available technology
such as small drones, in which anything, anywhere can become
a target.” This, she went on to say, raised “urgent
questions” about NATO’s own preparations in the face of
such an attack.

Before mighty odds and expensive
machinery, new methods of war are proving resourceful,
daring and devastating. One palpable absurdity of the Iran
War has been the eye-popping costs accruing from the use of
heavy weaponry in offence and anti-ballistic missiles such
as the THAAD system in defence. This has drained the US
inventory, sending Washington’s allies into fits of
concern. On a relatively meagre budget, labouring in the
face of superior odds and numbers, Tehran has caused mayhem
with its drone and missile strikes across the Gulf region.
In the case of RAF Fairford, the Iranians, whatever the
speculation, did not even need to launch a single drone for
an expensive fleet of bombers to be relocated to the
continental US.

Despite no official confirmation that
Tehran was actually involved, the commentary circuit
has been clogged by assessments of a victory for the Islamic
Republic. “I think it is hard to conclude anything other
than that this will be seen as a success by Iran,” suggests
former UK first national security advisor, Lord Peter
Ricketts. “Whether it was the intention or whether it’s
the inadvertent outcome, it is certainly the outcome that
they have now forced the US into a public bring-back of
their forces from one of their allies.”
