the crucial lesson: “that in an age of drone warfare, it
is no longer sufficient to assume that aircraft parked in
the open are invulnerable to attack.” The US needed “to
invest in hardening bases, including developing new hardened
aircraft shelters for forward deployed aircraft.” Another,
surely cheaper solution would be to refrain from launching
criminally foolish wars in the Middle East, or anywhere
else, for that matter.

The war against Iran was meant
to conclude in a popular insurrection against the theocrats
in Tehran and the blooming of various flowers in the
Orangerie of democracy. There was no insurrection and
certainly no flowering. Instead, the successor regime to
those slayed continues to resist with steeliness and wage
its battle in the fields of briefings, psychology and
economics. So far, it is winning.

news.text: STRASBOURG/LYON/PARIS: Demonstrations swept across France on Tuesday as teachers and parents took to the streets with high school pupils on the biggest day of what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described as the most ​violent student demonstrations in decades.Police fired tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups on the fringes of marches in Paris, Strasbourg, Rennes and Toulouse, among other cities. news.title: Behind closed doors: The grim data that has campaigns freaking out
news.text:
In the elections when President Donald Trump has been on the ballot, he and his fellow Republicans have often exceeded expectations in the polls. Yet according to a pollster Sarah Longwell from The Bulwark, Democrats and other Trump opponents who fear that he will again outperform the polls — which for the upcoming midterm elections place his party at a major disadvantage — should not succumb to their "PTSD."

"Most of us should have enough polling PTSD to be cautious in how bullish we are about Dems destroying GOP candidates next month," Longwell posted on X. 'The biggest indicators for me are candidate behavior and where money is being spent. And Republicans are clearly freaking out at their internals and are having to spend money in all kinds of places that should be safe for them."

This is not Longwell's first analysis which has offered a dire prognosis for Republicans.

"The overwhelming vibe among Trump voters in our focus groups is depression," Longwell wrote in September. "Trump isn’t doing what he said he would! And depressed voters = depressed turnout. It’s not that so many Republicans are going to vote for Democrats, it’s that so many Republicans aren’t going to vote."

She also described how Trump compares to the "Bush line," or the moment when Bush was in the low 30s and 20s near the end of his presidency that is considered as unpopular as a president can be — that is, unpopular with everyone except his own party's hardcore base.

"And so for me, I think there's a bunch of things that Trump being well below the Bush line would do," Longwell explained. "One, it would say that this was a failure, the MAGA experiment was a failure. Two, it would hang around. We want Trump's presidency to hang around future Republicans like J.D. Vance, like Marco Rubio, like an albatross. We don't want it to be a thing that bolsters him. But also the lower he is going into the midterms, like right now, Gallup's got him at 33 percent."

When she interviewed Republican voters on another occasion in September, Longwell admitted that they seemed "depressed" with the state of their party under Trump.

"At first, Trump voters—even ones who’d supported him twice—were genuinely shaken," Longwell said. "I did a couple of focus groups six days after January 6, 2021, in the aftermath of Trump supporters violently storming the U.S. Capitol in an attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 election, which Trump told them had been rigged."

"One group was with women who voted for Trump in both 2016 and 2020, and another was with women who’d voted for Trump in 2016 and then switched to Biden. In the two-time-Trump-voter group, Jamie from Pennsylvania said she was 'appalled' and 'shocked' by what she saw," Longwell added. “I realized, but yet I didn’t, if that makes any sense, that there are people out there that could do that.”

Longwell then broke down one person she interviewed.

"Audra from Arizona said, 'I think the reason he should be impeached is really just so that he can’t run ever again.' Trump was impeached the next day," Longwell wrote. "The Trump-to-Biden group was similarly harsh. Like Tina from Pennsylvania: 'The windows were being cracked, people were being killed, I don’t understand how this happened like this. And if he’s behind it, they really should impeach him, get rid of it and that’s it.' For a brief moment, reality was undeniable, and people’s opinions of Trump became soft and changeable."

news.title: 4 takeaways from the first debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
news.text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson faced off in a televised debate on Tuesday, sparring over a wide range of topics, including President Donald Trump, high prices and corruption allegations. 

It was the first of four debates scheduled for the next two weeks.

Independent polling shows a tight race. Jackson, a 59-year-old former logger and state Senate president, holds a two-point lead over the 73-year-old Collins, according to polling averages from FiftyPlusOne.

But a Marist poll released on Tuesday had Jackson up, 51% to 47%, with only 1% undecided. The Democrat’s four-point lead was just outside of the margin of error of +/- 3.8 percentage points.

Here are a few takeaways from the high-stakes showdown. 

1. The candidates blamed each other for the high cost of living

The high costs of living — especially gasoline and home heating prices — have repeatedly been cited by voters as their top concern leading up to the midterms.

So it’s no surprise that Jackson and Collins tried to blame each other for the situation. 

Jackson, perhaps, had the easiest line of attack. Throughout the night, Jackson repeatedly tied Collins to Trump and his unpopular policies and actions, including tariffs, the war with Iran and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025, which cut healthcare and other safety net programs and gave tax breaks the the wealthy.

Collins, however, pushed back, saying for example that Jackson was cherry-picking one analysis showing she voted with Trump more than 95% of the time. Other analyses showed a much lower rate, she said, noting that she’s not close with the president.

She then raised the issue of high property taxes and electricity rates, saying “those are all due to Augusta’s failed policies under the failed leadership of Troy Jackson,” who served six years as Senate president. 

2. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was in the spotlight.

Jackson repeatedly blamed Collins for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made permanent tax cuts for the wealthy while making deep cuts to healthcare and safety net programs.

Collins voted to advance the Republican bill to the Senate floor, but voted against enacting it. 

Jackson used Collins’ vote advancing the measure to cast her as being on the side of billionaires.

“Senator Collins has had 30 years to show whose side she’s on,” he said. “I don’t owe Donald Trump or the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does. I owe Mainers everything, and that’s who I’m gonna be fighting for when I’m the next U.S. senator.”

Collins criticized Jackson for distorting her record. She said she only voted to advance the bill so she could help author an amendment inserting a $50 billion fund to help rural hospitals. She said she voted against the final measure’s enactment because of the Medicaid cuts it contained. But the bill passed after Vice President JD Vance cast a tiebreaking vote.

Jackson said that reasoning wasn’t good enough.

“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said.

3. The candidates accused each other of corruption.

Collins has been under fire for nearly two weeks since ProPublica published a report detailing allegations that she was leveraging her role on the appropriations committee to solicit political donations. The outlet reported the FBI was gearing up for an investigation into Collins’ circle until Trump returned to office in 2025 and disbanded certain anti-corruption units.

Collins defended herself Tuesday, pointing out that she had advocated for a project involving the defense contractor Navatek at the urging of the University of Maine — not at the urging of a donor.

Collins then accused Jackson of corruption, raising questions about a mortgage he signed and reimbursements he got while serving in the Legislature. 

Jackson said he signed a mortgage document stating that his second home in Augusta would be his primary residence — which he said he was advised to do since he would spend more than half of the year there.

But a home in Allagash remained his permanent residence as defined by the state law. Jackson said he would travel there every weekend from Augusta, leading to his expense reimbursements.

4. Jackson was aggressive. Collins was knowledgeable.

Throughout the debate, Collins displayed her experience and knowledge of federal policies. She repeatedly called out Jackson for suggesting her committee had authority over things it does not, such as Medicaid rates.

Jackson, meanwhile, was relentless in going after Collins’ record. He criticized her for supporting Brett Kavanaugh’s appointment to the U.S. Supreme Court and for standing behind that vote after the court overturned the federal abortion protections under Roe v. Wade.

And he continued to hammer Collins for voting to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and for supporting Trump’s agenda, despite Collins’ efforts to highlight instances where she has broken with the president — such as her moves to push back against his tariffs and against his administration’s efforts to cut medical research funding.
news.summary: It was the first of 4 meetings between the candidates in the next 2 weeks.

news.title: The real reason Trump’s second term is spinning out of control: biographer
news.text:
A journalist who has written four biographies of President Donald Trump, Michael Wolff, told a podcast on Tuesday that he and other Trump experts are surprised at how rapidly he has self-destructed since the start of his second term.

"Donald Trump’s narcissistic impulses have set the stage for the 'first act' of the president’s 'downfall,' says his longtime biographer.'It is hard to truly express how bad things are for Donald Trump at this point,' author Michael Wolff told the Inside Trump’s Head podcast," reported The Daily Beast's Erkki Forster on Tuesday.

"Wolff said even Tony Schwartz, the remorseful ghostwriter behind Trump’s 1987 book The Art of the Deal, whom he called 'one of those people who really understand Donald Trump,' told him he has been left stunned by how Trump has been on a path of self-destruction in his second term," Forster added.

Speaking to his podcast co-host Joanna Coles, Wolff observed that "I think that that is now a pressing question. I mean, in terms of certainly trying to understand Donald Trump and possibly in terms of understanding what may be this turn in history. Why is Donald Trump so self-destructive?”

He speculated that when Trump resumed office last year, he was determined to pursue his personal agendas without regard to the political consequences.

“The story of our podcast, now slightly more than a year old, is that he charged into this second term with more aggression, more venom, more determination than almost any president, certainly in modern memory, doing all sorts of things that were not thought out, in which he didn’t really make a political calculation on what their ultimate effect would be,” Wolff argued.

Now those chickens have come home to roost.

“‘OK, my numbers are sinking here. Obviously my immigration policies are incredibly unpopular. Having masked men in the streets; that’s not a good look. Shouldn’t I adjust that? The war in Iran, should I have gone into that? I’m a president who got elected on the promise of no more forever wars. Shouldn’t I have thought about that? Shouldn’t I have had an exit strategy?’” Wolff said. “I mean, this is where the self-destructive nature of this comes in.”

Earllier in October, Wolff argued that Trump may also be motivated in terms of his foreign policy by his fear about what Russian President Vladimir Putin might be able to prove about him.

“Steve Bannon and I were talking about what Putin might have on Trump, and Bannon went through all the things dismissing them," Wolff said. "He said, what I think he has on him are his college transcripts," which may prove that Trump struggled academically.

In September, Wolff argued that Trump has "departed reality," citing as an example his refusal to listen to experts about the threats posed by AI.

"What advisors are saying on a larger basis is he has departed reality," Wolff told Coles, continuing that Trump "can’t see clearly" that he should listen.

He continued, "In the case of the coming midterms, to deny that the Republicans are in serious trouble is again a departure from reality. So what the advisers, that is to say, the White House, and I detect Susie Wiles' hand in this... are taking issue with the president and with this president. Now, remember, these people know that he is Donald Trump, that he is mercurial, that he is, that he doesn't listen to people. They know this. They're used to this. So what they are saying is that this goes beyond that. We're in new territory."

news.title: Russia Denies Anti-Plague Measures After Pneumonia Death
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Russia denied claims that it was imposing anti-plague measures following the death of a laboratory technician of pneumonic plague.The woman worked at the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region.The authorities in Russia, however, said the cause of death is yet to be confirmed, and Moscow's health authority Rospotrebnadzor has denied claims the country had put special measures in place.Authorities deny reports of plagueAccording to Rospotrebnadzor, the information "does not originate from official sources" and is "untrue," with Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev adding that the inspection had found that the woman's death was a result of pneumonia."No microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples," he said.Plague is a disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, known to be the most contagious and potentially fatal if not treated early.Some reports in Russia suggested the woman could have caught the disease from a broken test tube, while others speculated on a potential link between her death and a lab accident at the institute.The woman may have come into contact with up to 200 people, all of whom are under quarantine, according to one report.World Health Organization monitoring situationThe World Health Organization (WHO) said the information it had received from Russia suggests that "no case" of the disease has so far been recorded in Irkutsk. Russia has launched an epidemiological investigation into a case of pneumonia, labeled as "community acquired," in an employee at the Irkutsk Institute."Test results showed no presence of dangerous infectious disease pathogens" in the people who came into contact with the person, the WHO said, adding that the agency estimates the risk to be "moderate to low" for Irkutsk.The WHO is still monitoring the situation closely, it said.US President Donald Trump said he will discuss the case with Russian President Vladimir Putin.Trump also said the US intelligence is in "very deep discussions" on the matter, while also calling the disease "rough.""That's a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” the US president told reporters at the White House.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington is monitoring the situation.According to Rubio, Russia needs to "share more information with the world."Read: Pneumonic Plague in Russia: What Is It and How Dangerous Is It?Click here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News
